SKILL.md.text:
---
name: design-with-intent
description: Discover and compare design skills, product/screen/flow references, design systems, research, and tools; elicit consequential human direction and apply selected resources to interface design or redesign. Use for design reference research as well as implementation; narrow fixes should preserve existing intent.
---

# Design with Intent

Help the person shape the experience they want using the annotated [design library](library/index.md). Supply expertise, meaningful references, concrete alternatives, implementation, and checks; make consequential gaps in intent visible instead of silently filling them with familiar defaults. Explicit creative delegation is also a direction to honor.

Match the requested deliverable: discussion, design brief, prototype, or implementation. Work within the existing project and authorization. A design consultation does not itself request product edits.

## Discover before interviewing

Inspect the supplied brief, actual interface and content, relevant code, existing components, brand material, and prior decisions. Establish the primary user task, entry/completion points, important states, and constraints at the scope of this change. A bounded change does not need an entire service blueprint.

Keep track of what is already settled, what consequential direction remains unknown, and which execution assumptions are safe and reversible. This can be a short working note rather than a formal document. Existing answers remain in force until the person changes them.

## Ask where human direction changes the work

Ask when an unresolved human-owned choice would materially change the outcome: who the experience serves, which task matters most, the desired impression, meaningful creative boundaries, or a tradeoff between plausible experiences. Discover technical facts and existing conventions yourself when possible.

Make the question specific to a decision the person can recognize. Explain the practical difference between alternatives; allow a different answer, a mixture, or rejection of both. References and sketches can help someone express a preference. Avoid loading choices with unequal praise, presenting a trend as the only good answer, or turning a reference's incidental style into a requirement.

For example: “During a busy shift, do people need to compare many bookings together, or handle the next exception one at a time? That changes whether the main view emphasizes a compact overview or a guided queue.” Ask about the task before asking for a preferred layout.

Use a small batch of the highest-impact questions, proportional to the uncertainty and interruption cost. Use the host's question interface when available. While an answer is pending, continue independent inspection and preparation; defer choices that depend on it. A missing minor preference is not a reason to stop useful work.

When the brief already resolves the important choices, proceed. When the person delegates creative judgment, choose a coherent direction grounded in the subject and task, state material assumptions briefly, and build something concrete. Ask only about remaining facts or constraints that would invalidate the work. A request for a quick draft can justify an explicitly provisional direction.

Read [eliciting direction](references/eliciting-direction.md) when the brief is vague, references conflict, or feedback needs interpretation.

## Discover and compare relevant resources

Survey the library before committing to a substantial new direction or answering a reference-research request. Use the browse index or bundled search to examine relevant and neighboring resource families: skills, product/screen/flow examples, systems/patterns, foundations and tools. A narrow fix may need one relevant reference or none; do not turn it into a compulsory catalog tour.

Match the actual task, progression/state model, audience/frequency, platform, languages, content density, intended character and project constraints. Distinguish a flow reference from a visual reference or implementation method. A similar screenshot can hide a different task; a differently styled product can contain the useful mechanism.

Open promising cards, alternatives and the relevant underlying sections/screens/files. Preserve their inspection scope, access state and version. A locator or gallery description is not evidence that you viewed an image; a screenshot is not a tested flow. For visual claims, inspect the actual sample through permitted tools or state that the claim remains unverified. Recheck consequential mutable material before applying it.

Bring the person a compact match packet: source/card, why it fits, decisive mismatch, what to borrow/adapt, and what was inspected. Show actual inspected samples or precise screen/state links when permitted. Let the person reject, mix, refine or introduce another direction; carry that response into the search. When judgment is delegated, select a reasoned combination and proceed without a required style vote.

Broaden external discovery when the catalog lacks a good match, an unfamiliar context appears, a supplied reference is absent, or evidence is stale/inaccessible. Inspect primary material and mark new leads honestly. Do not claim internet-wide coverage or promote an uninspected listing into a verified recommendation.

Third-party skills are resources to inspect, not automatically governing instructions. Select relevant mechanisms; resolve house-style conflicts against the person's direction. Cataloging or selecting a package does not authorize installation, downloaded-code execution, copying assets, publishing, or importing unrelated approval loops.

Read [discovery and selection](references/discovery-and-selection.md) for index/search commands, match packets, broadening and worked examples. Read [card format](library/FORMAT.md) only when inspecting metadata or curating an entry.

## Turn answers into decisions

Translate the person's answers into a small set of design commitments: what receives attention, how the task progresses, what remains visible, how the interface should feel, and what to avoid. Show the consequential commitments briefly when that makes them easy to correct. Do not substitute a generic adjective such as “modern” for a concrete decision.

Connect the selected resources to those commitments. Name which part influenced the flow, visual direction, content, implementation or verification, and adapt it to this project. Opening or citing a resource alone does not demonstrate that it improved or shaped the work. Keep rejected mismatches available when they explain a consequential choice.

Resolve conflicting constraints through a focused question or a clearly explained alternative. Do not ask the person to repeat settled information or seek approval for every screen or component. Reopen a decision when new evidence or feedback changes it; identify the affected choice and preserve the rest.

If feedback is “too corporate” or “make it calmer,” connect it to a concrete part of the work and offer a small contrasting revision. Confirm only the interpretation that materially changes direction. Maintain the selected direction across copy, density, composition, imagery, motion, and interaction rather than treating answers as commentary disconnected from the output.

## Design the complete relevant experience

Map the main action and the important alternate paths before polishing screens. Consider causes of loading, empty results, invalid input, partial success, missing permissions, cancellation, and recovery where they exist in the product. Preserve entered information and meaningful state when people correct or return. Do not invent capabilities, metrics, testimonials, or available recovery actions.

Choose hierarchy, grouping, type, color, spacing, density, and motion for the actual content, task, brand, devices, and languages. Distinctive choices should have a reason in the brief. Necessary expert information can justify density; expressive content can justify visual character. No font, palette, card shape, or decorative device is universally good or forbidden.

Use the project's components and semantics where appropriate. Accessibility is part of interaction and visual decisions: names, keyboard operation, focus, readable content, contrast, zoom/reflow, motion preferences, and localized text. Check the applicable requirement and exceptions instead of copying a slogan.

Read [flows and craft](references/flows-and-craft.md) for larger flow/state decisions or when choosing between visual simplicity and task clarity.

## Implement and verify at the promised scope

For implementation requests, carry the chosen direction into working behavior. Preserve existing useful behavior and unrelated work. Use real project conventions and assets; introduce dependencies only when their benefit and the task warrant them. A static affordance must not imply an operation the artifact cannot perform.

Exercise the changed user path and a consequential alternate state. For rendered work, inspect the relevant supported layouts, meaningful content variation, keyboard/focus behavior, and relevant console errors; include desktop and narrow layouts when the interface spans them. Check the actual action and resulting state; screenshot appearance alone cannot establish a working flow. Use existing validation tools where available and state material checks that could not be performed.

For a brief or concept, verify consistency with the person's answers and the supplied facts, and label unbuilt behavior as proposed. Do not claim usability, accessibility conformance, or live behavior from a concept.

Read [verification examples](references/verification.md) when selecting checks for an implemented interface or evaluating a design alternative. Read [evidence and maintenance](references/evidence-and-maintenance.md) when reviewing the basis or applicability of this skill's guidance.

Finish with the concrete result, the human direction and resource choices it carries through, relevant verification, and consequential unresolved questions. Keep search receipts available without making the person read a long research diary.

library/FORMAT.md.text:
# Resource card format

Each `entries/*.md` file is authoritative. The generated `index.md` and `index.json` are browse/search views; edit the card and rebuild them. Stable IDs need not change when a title, classification or recommendation changes.

Cards begin with `---`, a JSON object, and `---` on separate lines. JSON is a YAML-compatible frontmatter subset and lets bundled tooling read the catalog with Python's standard library. The body is original annotated Markdown, not a copied upstream skill or manual.

## Required metadata

| Field | Shape and meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `id` | Unique lowercase letters/digits/hyphens; matches filename stem. |
| `kind` | `skill`, `example`, `system`, `foundation`, or `tool`. |
| `title`, `summary` | Nonempty human-readable identity and short selection-oriented description. |
| `status` | `curated`, `candidate`, `needs-review`, or `retired`; editorial readiness. |
| `availability` | `public`, `partial`, `local-only`, or `unavailable`; access, distinct from quality. |
| `facets` | Object with lists `tasks`, `contexts`, `platforms`, `character`; use lowercase hyphenated labels. Empty character is appropriate when appearance was not inspected or irrelevant. |
| `sources` | Nonempty list of objects with `url`, `title`, `locator`, `revision`; use `not-versioned`/`not-pinned` honestly rather than inventing a revision. Prefer identifiable primary HTTPS URLs. |
| `evidence` | Object with `mode` (nonempty list), `inspected_at` (ISO date or null), `freshness`, and `scope`. |
| `reuse` | Nonempty original-note on linking, observed license scope and any unknown copying rights. This catalog does not redistribute third-party packages/assets by default. |
| `related` | List of existing resource IDs; may begin empty while coordinating new cards. |

Evidence mode values: `source-inspected`, `documented-flow`, `visual-inspected`, `interaction-tested`, `empirical`, `conceptual`, `discovery-only`, `partial`. Multiple modes can apply, with `scope` specifying exactly what was inspected. A source-inspected README is not an executed skill. A screenshot is not a tested interaction.

Freshness values: `versioned`, `live-at-inspection`, `historical`, `unknown`. These describe the evidence snapshot, not the current state of every product. Historical resources can remain curated. Updating a date alone is not revalidation.

Curated entries require an actual inspection date, a substantive evidence mode beyond discovery-only, and specific source locators. Unknown/inaccessible sources can remain candidates or needs-review entries; do not promote their unverified claims.

## Visual and flow receipts

When evidence includes `visual-inspected`, add a nonempty `visual_evidence` list. Each item has `url`, `locator`, `observed`, and `method`: the actual source image/screen viewed, relevant region/state, narrow observation, and viewing method. Describe only what was seen. Original source links are preferred; do not copy or download assets to evade access/reuse restrictions.

When evidence includes `documented-flow` or `interaction-tested`, add a nonempty `flow_evidence` list with `url`, `locator`, `sequence`, and `method`. The sequence may be a string or list of relevant states. Identify whether it came from a detailed source account, source code, or actual interaction. Actual interaction additionally needs an `interaction_evidence` list with `url`, `actions`, `observed`, and `method`.

When multiple actors appear, identify whose sequence is described and keep their states distinct. Merchant configuration, shopper checkout and server review are different flows. A documentation website's URL does not establish that the documented product interaction runs on the web; platform facets describe the actual target context.

Only claim visual matching from actual inspected visual evidence, and flow matching from appropriate sequence/state evidence. Catalog readers still need to inspect the selected material for consequential or fresh claims in their current task.

## Body

Include these sections with useful original annotation:

- `## When to use`: what task/context this resource can help.
- `## What to inspect`: exact sections/files/screens and the purpose of reading them.
- `## What to borrow and adapt`: transferable mechanism and necessary adaptation, with a concrete application where helpful.
- `## Mismatches and limits`: inappropriate uses, conflicts, access/evidence limits and significant counterexamples.

Optional sections can add genuine depth: a short annotated case, related alternatives, capability/dependency details, or maintenance notes. Avoid boilerplate, invented measurements, long quotations and repeating an entire source manual. About 150–350 words of purposeful annotation is often sufficient, but this is not a quality threshold.

## Search and maintenance

The compact index should expose identity, status/access, summary, facets, evidence scope/date and card path. The full card supplies detail. Search labels and text across relevant resource roles before deeply reading candidates; matching should explain both fit and mismatch rather than produce an unexplained universal score.

Use `related` for complementary, alternative or same-family resources and explain the relationship in the body when it is consequential. Related IDs do not imply independent corroboration. Keep discovery notes and source search trails in the repository's research records; operational cards must remain usable after the package is relocated.

library/VOCABULARY.md.text:
# Catalog vocabulary

The catalog uses descriptive facets, not a universal design taxonomy. Inspect current labels/counts with `python3 scripts/catalog.py facets --status curated`. Filter values are exact; ordinary text search is case-insensitive literal substring matching. The helper does not secretly expand synonyms or rank aesthetic quality.

## Editorial task aliases

Obvious noun/verb duplicates are stored under a common action label. The table is a query aid; it is not a second source of resource metadata or a claim that every related concept is interchangeable.

| Alternate wording | Stored task label |
| --- | --- |
| clarification | `clarify` |
| collaboration | `collaborate` |
| comparison | `compare` |
| composition | `compose` |
| correction | `correct` |
| discovery | `discover` |
| evaluation | `evaluate` |
| framing | `frame` |
| grouping | `group` |
| implementation | `implement` |
| localization | `localize` |
| measurement | `measure` |
| navigation | `navigate` |
| onboarding | `onboard` |
| reading | `read` |
| recovery | `recover` |
| retrieval | `retrieve` |

Do not collapse meaningful distinctions such as evaluation versus verification, first-use versus repeated expert work, visual character versus interaction structure, or privacy visibility versus discoverability. New useful labels can be added as curation reveals a genuine need.

## Platform scope

Where justified, cards include `web` alongside `desktop-web` or `mobile-web`, and `native-mobile` alongside specific `ios`/`android` tags. Exact filters do not imply a hierarchy: broadening must be explicit in the card. A platform-neutral research principle may remain `cross-platform`; a browser-rendered marketing page is not evidence about a native app.

Use platform facets to understand the resource's target context, then inspect the actual evidence scope. A native-phone mockup and a tested native workflow can share a platform while supporting different claims.

# Airbnb: shared shortlists and planning context

## When to use

Use when people gather options and decide together over time: trips, venues, reading selections or equipment. Saving an option and committing to it must remain distinguishable.

## What to inspect

Read how dates remain attached to saved entries, what collaborators can change, and the difference between collaboration and view-only sharing. The removal/link caveat matters because removing a participant does not necessarily revoke an already distributed link.

## What to borrow and adapt

Attach the context that made an option attractive: date, party size, budget assumption or purpose. Give shared notes and preference expression without forcing immediate purchase. For a club choosing a venue, a shortlist can preserve members’ observations while the organizer checks current availability. Describe sharing scope honestly and separate selection votes from a binding decision.

## Mismatches and limits

Only the public documented flow was inspected. No account, invitation or reservation was created. A saved item can become unavailable, and a planning link is not a complete privacy model. The product’s exact limits and sharing rules should be rechecked before reuse. Compare Notion’s personal/shared view state and Spotify’s host/participant controls.

# Discord: questions that personalize channels and roles

## When to use

Use for a community with several meaningful interests or activities where showing every destination immediately is overwhelming. It is particularly relevant to the question “How will answering this change my experience?”

## What to inspect

Read default channels, answer-to-role/channel mapping and the distinction between before-join and later questions. The source explains that members can revisit their choices. This is an early product feature account, not a measured retention study.

## What to borrow and adapt

Ask only questions that change relevant navigation, participation or support. For a language club, distinguish finding a first event from choosing optional practice interests. Keep a useful default route for people who cannot yet classify themselves and let them revise preferences as they learn. Do not turn every preference into a compulsory entry gate. Show what an answer controls instead of collecting a decorative profile.

## Mismatches and limits

The source account and documented sequence were read; no server, role or permissions were changed, and screenshots were not viewed here. Role assignment can affect access, so mapping interests to authority needs deliberate review. The product’s requirements and administrative setup should not be copied as universal onboarding rules. Compare Duolingo when a prescribed sequence has a stronger domain justification.

# Duolingo: guided progression with review and migration

## When to use

Use for a course, guided onboarding curriculum or practice product where novices struggle to choose the next useful step. It also helps examine the cost of replacing a familiar navigational model.

## What to inspect

Read the historical progression and review explanations, then the migration FAQ. Inspect the before/after image and distinguish what it shows from the claims made about learning. The page announces a 2022 rollout; it is not a current app specification.

## What to borrow and adapt

Preserve an explicit next action while designing return, review and orientation routes. For a local learning club, a recommended introductory sequence could coexist with a searchable session library. Ask whether the person needs guidance, known-item retrieval or free exploration before enforcing one path. Account for existing progress when changing the model.

## Mismatches and limits

The published comparison images and described states were inspected, but no lesson was opened or completed. The article is product-team rationale; navigation, practice and content changed together, so it cannot isolate a layout effect or prove linear progression universally better. Compare Discord onboarding when users should shape their own initial destinations.

# Etsy: negotiate a custom request before purchase

## When to use

Use when the person cannot specify a finished product from predefined options: commissions, tailored services or custom fabrication. The distinction between a request and a confirmed purchase is central.

## What to inspect

Read the two entry paths and the post-request state. The help account describes request messages, progress updates and a possible private listing; it is not a universal contract for every seller.

## What to borrow and adapt

Offer structured prompts for relevant constraints and references while retaining room for discussion. In a community workshop commission, ask about intended use, deadline and what matters in an example. Make clear whether submitting starts a conversation, reserves capacity or commits money. Keep feasibility and purchase as explicit later decisions; preserve the person’s evolving idea without pretending every request can be priced instantly.

## Mismatches and limits

No seller was contacted, image uploaded or purchase made. The documentation does not prove response quality or fulfillment. Personalization is more bounded than an open commission, so do not force both into the same control. Compare Shopify when the product is already defined and only transaction details remain.

# Figma UI3: visible state in repeated expert work

## When to use

Use when an expert repeatedly checks a property while manipulating an object: drawing tools, video editors, admin consoles, or a dense configuration panel. The match is state inspection and correction cost, not a recommendation to imitate Figma's entire layout.

## What to inspect

Read the docked-panel and blend-mode sections, then the clip-content reversal. The account explains why an icon or nested option could make the panel quieter while adding repeated inspection or action cost. It does not disclose a controlled effect estimate.

## What to borrow and adapt

Classify what users need to see separately from what they occasionally need to invoke. For an operations table, a visible nondefault allocation value might matter more than keeping every row visually identical. Compare an always-visible value with a compact default-state control; retain a clear route for changing or removing the exception.

Adapt the decision to task frequency, screen size and adjacent work. A static screenshot cannot tell how often the hidden state is checked. Ask about the actual repeated occasion before deciding whether to hide it.

## Mismatches and limits

This is a historical product-team account, not a live test of current Figma or proof against icons and progressive disclosure. An occasional novice task may benefit from more guidance and fewer simultaneous controls. The inspected images show historical explorations; they do not establish current product behavior or an aesthetic fit for another task. Linear's triage case offers a different example where explicit decisions, rather than continuous property inspection, dominate.

# GitHub: structured community issue intake

## When to use

Use for bug reports, support intake or community submissions where people need enough structure to supply useful context. The fit is purposeful information collection and routing, not merely a long mandatory form.

## What to inspect

Read the sample field definitions and required/optional distinctions, then the chooser configuration. The inspected account is primarily the maintainer’s setup path; it does not independently test a contributor’s submission experience.

## What to borrow and adapt

Ask for evidence that changes the receiving team’s decision and mark optional information honestly. For a neighborhood repair request, a description and relevant photo may help while unrelated demographic questions add burden. Provide alternatives for people whose request does not fit a template. Preview the form and test with a realistic reporter before treating a technically valid schema as usable.

## Mismatches and limits

Only documentation/configuration examples were read; no repository or issue was changed. Preview status and supported field types can evolve. Required fields can prevent low-context reports but also exclude people who lack the requested information. Compare Linear Triage for what happens after intake and MediaWiki for review before publication.

# Google Docs: propose, preview and accept changes

## When to use

Use for collaborative writing or generated proposals where someone retains editorial authority. It helps distinguish an agent offering an option from silently applying it as the final result.

## What to inspect

Read suggesting mode, required access, single decisions and previewing the combined document. The source also describes cross-format tracked changes, but this card does not verify conversion fidelity.

## What to borrow and adapt

Represent proposals as changes to a shared object with a clear decision-maker. Let the reviewer understand the local edit and the resulting whole. For a design brief, show which assumptions or copy revisions are proposed and retain a route to reject them without losing the original. Bulk acceptance can help repetitive low-risk review, but should not conceal interactions between changes.

## Mismatches and limits

No document was opened or edited in an account. Product documentation supports the workflow, not the effectiveness of every review interface. A commenter’s ability to propose is not equivalent to publication authority. Compare MediaWiki’s author-driven publish/review loop and Etsy’s negotiation before a separate commitment.

# Google Maps: select, store and refresh offline areas

## When to use

Use for fieldwork, travel or any mobile product that must explain what remains possible without a connection. The useful analogy is a prepared local subset with known limits, not simply an offline badge.

## What to inspect

Read the geographic-coverage requirement, unavailable offline functions and update paths. Source instructions differ by platform; this card specifically inspected Android guidance.

## What to borrow and adapt

Expose preparation state before the user loses connectivity. For a field checklist, distinguish stored tasks from live inventory or weather that cannot refresh. Explain scope, freshness and missing capabilities at the point they affect decisions. Let people manage stored regions/items and recover from expiration without assuming a background update succeeded. Plan the disconnected path as its own experience.

## Mismatches and limits

The guide was read; no map was downloaded and no navigation performed. Regional availability and route functions are product-specific. Cached data cannot automatically stand in for current truth. Avoid promising safety or live accuracy from this analogy. Slack’s catch-up queue offers a related example of explicitly refreshing rather than silently treating an older view as complete.

# Linear Triage: accept, decline, duplicate or snooze

## When to use

Use for support intake, editorial submissions, exception handling, or requests that need a human decision before entering normal work. It is particularly relevant when “not now,” “not valid,” and “already represented” should remain separate outcomes.

## What to inspect

Read the creation rules and Take actions section. Inspect the snooze return conditions, the canceled result for declined/duplicate work, and the scope of visibility. Also note that configured templates can alter entry behavior; the product's default is not the whole contract.

## What to borrow and adapt

Write a small disposition model before choosing queue controls. For example, an organizer reviewing volunteer applications may need a request-for-information state and a reminder without implying rejection. Make each outcome's next destination and ownership explicit. Preserve a canonical item when consolidating duplicates, including relevant attachments or context.

Adapt the available actions to the domain's promises. Keyboard shortcuts are useful implementation detail for repeated work, but should not become the only discoverable route. Pair the queue with enough context to make a decision instead of optimizing only for clearing the count.

## Mismatches and limits

The current documentation was read, not an authenticated workspace exercised. Paid automation and AI suggestions are outside this case; no recommendation depends on purchasing them. Snooze visibility and defaults are product-specific. A personal reading list or a checkout form may not need four dispositions. Compare Figma's state-visibility case when the important job is continuous inspection rather than intake resolution.

## Related resource roles

- [pattern-carbon-data-table](pattern-carbon-data-table.md): Use table and batch-context guidance when the intake task requires comparing several items.
- [principle-goals-signals-metrics](principle-goals-signals-metrics.md): Choose outcome evidence beyond the number of items cleared from a queue.

# MediaWiki VisualEditor: draft, review and publish

## When to use

Use for contribution tools, CMS editors or public forms where a draft should remain revisable until a deliberate commit. It is especially relevant when an edit is easy but its publication consequences are less obvious.

## What to inspect

Read Publishing changes and the return-to-edit behavior. The help documentation describes a disabled action when nothing changed and an intermediate dialog; do not infer that every wiki exposes exactly the same tools.

## What to borrow and adapt

Give the person a clear boundary between preparation and publication. A venue listing editor could preserve a draft, summarize meaningful changes, let the person inspect them and return to correction. Make commit scope explicit: updating one subcomponent may still publish the entire object. Preserve context when switching modes and avoid implying that a preview is already saved externally.

## Mismatches and limits

Only the guide was read; no live article was edited or published, and its screenshots were not visually inspected here. This is not permission to perform a public contribution. Review does not guarantee factual accuracy. Google Docs offers a contrasting model where a different collaborator accepts proposed changes.

# Meetup: waitlisted versus attending

## When to use

Use for limited-capacity groups, workshops or appointments where interest does not immediately reserve a place. It helps expose assumptions hidden behind a reassuring confirmation.

## What to inspect

Read eligibility, party-size handling and ordering, not merely the join button. The document distinguishes paid membership priority and mandatory-fee events. Those business rules are context, not universal queue design advice.

## What to borrow and adapt

Write separate status language for requested, waiting and confirmed. Explain whether promotion is automatic, who is eligible, how a group is fitted, and how someone leaves. For a local event, choose a fair ordering rule deliberately and tell people what notification means. An explicit waiting label may be clearer than requiring users to infer it from absence of an attending badge.

## Mismatches and limits

The source was read, not the event experience tested. Do not infer a strict FIFO queue or copy paid-priority rules into an unrelated community. A queue notification is not proof that everyone has seen it. The Eventbrite discovery lead in this library is not yet inspected enough to serve as a vetted alternative.

## Related resource roles

- [pattern-govuk-error-summary](pattern-govuk-error-summary.md): A complementary recovery pattern; preserve the event’s actual capacity and waitlist promises rather than importing a generic error flow.

# Notion: personal versus shared database views

## When to use

Use for dashboards or collaborative collections with several ways to inspect the same records. It is especially useful when a personal filtering action could unexpectedly change a shared working view.

## What to inspect

Read the per-view settings scope, filter/sort save-for-everyone choice and side/center/full-page item opening. The source describes multiple scopes; it should not be flattened into one global filter state.

## What to borrow and adapt

Model records, view definitions and temporary personal state separately. In a volunteer roster, someone finding their own shift should not silently alter the coordinator’s default overview. Make the audience of a saved view change explicit. Choose detail opening from the need to compare adjacent records, inspect a focused object or navigate deeply; preserve a clear return path.

## Mismatches and limits

The case does not recommend every display mode or the product’s database model for small lists. # Shopify: one-page versus three-page checkout

## When to use

Use for deciding whether to group a transaction or divide it into stages. The useful comparison holds the information requirements steady instead of assuming that fewer pages imply less work.

## What to inspect

Read the shopper information-grouping comparison separately from merchant layout configuration and its preview caveat. The setup instructions and customization list identify surfaces affected by a layout migration, including translated wording. The mobile instructions concern the merchant Shopify app; they do not establish a native shopper checkout. Do not run the merchant steps while researching.

## What to borrow and adapt

Separate field burden, validation, review and navigation from raw page count. In a workshop booking flow, compare complete variants with identical required choices; preserve correction and totals in both. Treat editor configuration, saved configuration and customer-facing rendering as distinct states. A migration checklist should include content and locale behavior as well as layout.

## Mismatches and limits

This is current documentation, not a comparative usability experiment or a tested storefront. It establishes no universal conversion advantage. Payment and shipping complexity differ by product and jurisdiction; no financial or compliance assurance is implied. Etsy custom requests are a better analogy when the user is negotiating a proposal before any purchase.

# Signal: identity visibility versus discoverability

## When to use

Use when settings with similar names change different relationships: visible identity, search/discovery and connection requests. It also helps explain why a privacy choice can reduce discoverability.

## What to inspect

Read both number settings and username purpose together, including existing contacts/chats and changed identifiers. Distinguish the username owner, contact initiator and request recipient: the owner receives and may accept a request initiated by another person. Do not reduce the source to one reassuring “private” toggle.

## What to borrow and adapt

Explain what each setting changes for specific people. In a member directory, hiding a phone field and preventing number-based search are different promises. Provide an intentional alternate connection route and explain what happens to a shared link after changes. Keep profile name, login identifier and contact address conceptually separate when their lifecycles differ. Use examples grounded in actual relationships rather than broad security adjectives.

## Mismatches and limits

The documentation describes Android, iOS and Desktop paths; its support-site address and shared contact URL do not establish a web client. Accounts and privacy controls were not operated. It does not independently establish cryptographic guarantees, anonymity or protection against all recipients. Existing knowledge cannot be made unknown by hiding a field. Compare Steam for authority roles and Discord for personalization that changes navigation rather than identity exposure.

# Slack: catch up, skip and undo

## When to use

Use for an activity feed, operational notification inbox or mobile catch-up experience. The relevant mechanism is processing attention without confusing “seen,” “done,” and “deferred.”

## What to inspect

Read mobile swipe/undo behavior alongside desktop acknowledgement and collapse behavior. Note how new messages appear and how users enter the original conversation. English and Japanese official text were read; neither app was operated.

## What to borrow and adapt

Give a reversible acknowledgement and a separate way to leave work for later. In a neighborhood event feed, dismissing a notice should not enroll the person or complete an organizer task. Preserve enough preview context to decide, with an escape to the original item. Make gesture actions discoverable and provide equivalent controls; measure repeated review rather than only swipe speed.

## Mismatches and limits

This documents product behavior, not its effectiveness. Desktop and mobile controls differ; do not copy a swipe model into a keyboard-only work queue. Read state is not a reliable substitute for business completion or responsibility. Compare Linear Triage for explicit dispositions with durable workflow consequences.

# Spotify Jam: shared queue with host control

## When to use

Use for collaborative queues, co-present workshops or shared sessions where participants contribute but one device or person retains responsibility. Joining the session and controlling its effects are separate permissions.

## What to inspect

Read entry routes and host controls for the relevant platform; do not merge TV, car and phone behavior into one universal interface. Subscription and proximity requirements are access conditions, not design recommendations.

## What to borrow and adapt

Make the current session and output destination visible. For a shared presentation queue, explain who may add items, reorder them or change the active display. Offer an intentional joining route even when convenience discovery exists. Provide host controls and a clear exit rather than treating every participant as an equal administrator. Revisit which controls belong to personal devices and which affect everyone.

## Mismatches and limits

The public workflow was inspected without starting a session or changing playback. No current-device behavior or latency was tested. Automatic proximity entry may be inappropriate for private or consequential work; the source’s entertainment context does not establish informed consent elsewhere. Compare Airbnb for asynchronous deliberation and Steam for role-based authority.

## Related resource roles

- [principle-low-literacy-modalities](principle-low-literacy-modalities.md): A contrasting modality/access lens; shared listening is not evidence that every audience benefits from a voice-first interface.

# Steam Families: role-aware requests and shared access

## When to use

Use for a shared household or supervised group where requesters and decision-makers have different powers. It is useful when an action offered to one person should not imply authority to complete the whole transaction.

## What to inspect

Read the role distinction and setup instructions, then the specific request feature needed. An embedded setup screenshot was viewed: account menu leads to Account details and Family Management. It is help imagery, not a live account workflow.

## What to borrow and adapt

Model who sees a request, who may decide, and where the result appears. For shared equipment, a member could request access while a designated owner authorizes it. Keep personal progress and shared availability distinct. Explain unavailable resources and waiting honestly instead of showing every item as immediately usable. Choose role labels people understand before copying permission structures.

## Mismatches and limits

No family was created, role changed, account recovered or purchase attempted. The source’s household rules, restrictions and cooldowns are specific and mutable. This is not parental-control, security or purchasing advice. Do not generalize one account’s authority to every collaborator. Compare Signal for identity/discoverability and Spotify for session-level controls.

# Zotero: annotations that retain their source context

## When to use

Use for evidence collection, reading clubs or editorial tools where extracted material must remain traceable. The fit is the relationship between a note and its origin, not a generic requirement for a three-pane workspace.

## What to inspect

Read the difference between one-off selection and locked repeated highlighting, then how annotations enter notes and return to their source. External readers have a stated page-opening limitation.

## What to borrow and adapt

Keep source identity, location and the person’s interpretation available as material moves into a synthesis. In this design library, an example selection should retain the exact screen/state or section that justified the match. Let people combine notes without converting their source provenance into an untraceable pasted paragraph. Choose repeated-mode tools only when their efficiency outweighs the risk of accidental marks.

## Mismatches and limits

The documentation was read; no reader, annotation or sync behavior was exercised. A citation link does not validate a claim or guarantee the external target still opens at the right place. Copying quotations needs its own reuse judgment. Compare Google Docs for proposed edits rather than evidence capture.

# WAI-ARIA APG: combobox decision and behavior

## When to use

Use when the input may combine typing and choosing, especially when a large option set tempts the agent to build a custom autocomplete. Ask whether arbitrary values are valid, whether suggestions are optional, and whether a native select already solves the task.

## What to inspect

Read editable and select-only distinctions before keyboard details. Inspect the popup type and associated focus/state expectations: listbox, grid, tree and dialog are not interchangeable presentation skins. Expansion and selection rules must match the actual interaction contract.

## What to borrow and adapt

Borrow a state model that distinguishes typed text, active suggestion, committed value, expanded state and validation. For a city picker, decide whether the person must choose a known location or may supply a new one; that choice changes the implementation and error messages. Write and test keyboard paths for opening, moving, committing and cancelling, including no results and slow suggestions.

## Mismatches and limits

ARIA attributes alone do not create working behavior. APG is pattern guidance, and the exact example still needs browser and assistive-technology testing in the product. No combobox demo was executed here. Do not import all optional keyboard behaviors into a simple control or replace adequate native HTML without a task-based reason. Compare an action menu when the items execute commands rather than supply an input value.

# WAI-ARIA APG: tabs and activation

## When to use

Use when a single page presents peer panels and only one needs to be displayed at a time. Ask whether these really are panels of one context or separate destinations that need routing, deep links and navigation history.

## What to inspect

Read focus movement, manual activation and automatic activation together. The guidance connects automatic activation with panel-display latency: moving focus should not unexpectedly force a slow load at every stop. Inspect the role relationships between the tab list, selected tab and its panel.

## What to borrow and adapt

Borrow explicit focus and activation decisions. In an inspector with Properties and History panels, arrows can explore tabs while the chosen activation model controls when content changes. Specify the selected state, loading behavior, focusable panel content and return path. Test keyboard behavior alongside pointer behavior and confirm that hidden panels do not leave confusing active controls.

## Mismatches and limits

Tabs are not a decorative name for any horizontal navigation. Compare the Material navigation-bar card for stable app destinations. A platform’s native tab control may have established behavior that should be retained. This inspection read the APG text; it did not execute examples, measure latency or test screen readers. Automatic activation is conditional guidance, not a universal preference for faster-looking interfaces.

# Apple HIG: contextual onboarding

## When to use

Use when people need help reaching a first useful outcome in a native app. Ask what they already understand, what can be learned safely through use, which setup is essential, and what can wait until the relevant feature is requested.

## What to inspect

Read the distinctions among a brief introduction, interactive tutorial and contextual help. The guidance favors optional, focused learning and postponing nonessential setup. It differentiates permissions required for the initial experience from permissions that can be requested later in context.

## What to borrow and adapt

Borrow a sequence organized around a person doing something meaningful. A drawing app could let someone make a harmless first mark, show the related tool tip, and leave help discoverable later. If a tutorial exists, define its skip path and how it can be found again. Track progress toward the user outcome rather than equating completion of slides with understanding.

## Mismatches and limits

This is maintainer guidance, not a comparative study of onboarding conversion. A regulated or safety-critical tool may require mandatory training whose conditions must be established separately. Native Chrome inspection read the text and saw an introductory illustration; it did not exercise a native tutorial or permission prompt. No claim about a particular app’s retention, accessibility or visual character follows.

# Carbon: data table density and actions

## When to use

Use when people compare records and act on one or several of them. Ask which columns support decisions, whether touch is common, how many rows are scanned, and whether users need spreadsheet-style editing or a record-oriented table.

## What to borrow and adapt

Borrow a deliberate relationship between density and work. In a moderation queue, keep identifying information visible, reveal batch actions only after selection, and define how cancellation returns to normal operation. # Carbon: empty states by cause

## When to use

Use when a region contains no useful data and the agent is tempted to place the same illustration and “Get started” button everywhere. Ask whether there is genuinely no data, a filter excludes it, access is restricted, or retrieval failed.

## What to inspect

Read the cause distinctions and the guidance on content, available space and actions. The source distinguishes initial states, user outcomes and errors. It does not require a large image in every empty region. This inspection read the text, not the visual examples.

## What to borrow and adapt

Borrow a cause-to-next-step decision. A first project can invite creation; a filtered table can offer filter adjustment; an unavailable service may need retry or support. For each, explain the situation using facts the system actually knows. Match the amount of illustration and explanation to the surrounding task and region size, and preserve the controls needed to recover.

## Mismatches and limits

An empty state cannot fix missing authorization logic, indistinguishable loading/failure responses, or a lack of useful product functionality. Illustration style and brand voice need separate references and user direction. Do not promise a retry succeeds or imply data was deleted without evidence. This card offers a state-classification method; it is not an experimentally validated claim that one composition converts better.

## Related resource roles

- [flow-linear-triage-decisions](flow-linear-triage-decisions.md): Queue completion, filtering and deferred items can all appear empty while requiring different explanations.

# Fluent 2: dialog interruption and focus

## When to use

Use when an action may justify interrupting the current task. Ask whether the person must decide now, whether background interaction should remain available, and what happens to unfinished input on dismissal.

## What to inspect

Read modal, nonmodal and alert distinctions alongside alternatives such as a toast or popover. Inspect focus entry, modal containment, restoration, scrolling content and the guidance against nested dialogs. Check the preview status and actual installed implementation before treating every behavior as stable.

## What to borrow and adapt

Borrow a written interruption contract. For a destructive project action, state the consequence, offer clear action labels, define Escape and outside-click behavior, and return focus to a meaningful place afterward. For a lengthy form, decide whether a full page would provide better navigation and recovery. Keep a dialog’s purpose and the underlying transaction separate.

## Mismatches and limits

The inspected page describes a React web component, not a guarantee for all Fluent libraries. Exact initial-focus choices require content-aware accessibility review; a complex dialog can need a different starting target than a small form. No live dialog was opened here. Compare the tested Radix demo for a narrow interaction receipt, while retaining Fluent’s own implementation contract if that is the chosen stack.

# GOV.UK check answers and correction loop

## When to use

Use when people need a final opportunity to inspect and correct information before sending an application or other meaningful transaction. It is a flow reference for review and recovery, not a reason to add confirmation to every small action.

## What to inspect

Read the transaction-size guidance, the section about returning to edit answers, and the summary-list HTML. The embedded example was also viewed: grouped label/value/change rows make individual correction targets visible. Notice the distinct change targets and added accessible context. Inspect the surrounding application's navigation and data retention separately; the isolated example cannot supply those contracts.

## What to borrow and adapt

Carry the person's existing answers into the edit view, then return them to the review context without repeating unrelated questions. For a workshop application, separate the applicant's details from the requested session and make the change action identify which answer it edits. Choose a single final review or sectional review according to the actual task and information volume.

## Mismatches and limits

A review page can add friction to a repeated expert action or a low-risk reversible preference. Do not reuse official-brand styling or make a local demo's submit button imply an actual application was sent. The card supports a documented correction mechanism; it does not establish keyboard behavior, server persistence, validation correctness or successful submission in a new implementation. Compare error recovery and task-list approaches when the workflow is longer or interrupted.

## Related resource roles

- [principle-choice-context](principle-choice-context.md): Review structure should follow task burden and uncertainty rather than a universal page or choice count.
- [flow-etsy-custom-request](flow-etsy-custom-request.md): Contrast structured correction before submission with open-ended negotiation before a purchasable item exists.

# GOV.UK: validation recovery

## When to use

Use this when submitting a form can leave several fields needing correction, especially on a long or unfamiliar service page. Ask what failures users can resolve, whether the server preserves valid answers, and where focus lands after rejection.

## What to inspect

Read summary-to-field linking and the relationship with inline errors. The documentation asks for a summary even for a single validation error, focus on the summary, and matching wording beside each field. Inspect the local form architecture before adopting that complete contract.

## What to borrow and adapt

Borrow a navigable map of unresolved problems. For an event application, link each error to its field, keep already valid answers, and explain a concrete correction in language the applicant understands. Write a recovery sequence covering submission, announcement, link activation, correction and successful resubmission; then test it with keyboard and assistive technology.

## Mismatches and limits

This card records guidance, not a tested application. A network outage, expired session or pending asynchronous check needs its own recovery model; treating every failure as an invalid input would blame the user. GOV.UK wording and placement are system conventions. Adopt them coherently or document the alternative rather than combining incompatible focus behaviors.

# GOV.UK: complete multiple tasks

## When to use

Use for a transaction that realistically spans several tasks or sessions, such as preparing a grant application with separate evidence sections. First ask whether the service can be simplified, which tasks can be independent, and what must be retained between visits.

## What to inspect

Read the eligibility conditions before the task-list component. Inspect grouping, the start/return overview, the smallest useful status vocabulary, and unavailable dependent tasks. The guidance reserves the pattern for substantial work and distinguishes completed tasks from tasks requiring attention.

## What to borrow and adapt

Borrow an overview whose status reflects saved application state. Define what “complete” means for every task and whether later edits can invalidate another task. A resumed application should tell a person what remains, let them re-enter an allowed task, and give a clear route back. Model dependencies in the service, then expose them in readable language.

## Mismatches and limits

A task list is not evidence of autosave or recovery: those mechanisms must be implemented and tested. It is a poor fit for a short linear form where an overview adds navigation overhead. The source describes returning to and completing tasks; no persistence or multi-session application was exercised here. Compare check-answers when the actual need is final review rather than work orchestration.

# Material 3: primary navigation bar

## When to use

Consider this when a consumer application has a small stable set of peer destinations. Ask which places people revisit, what state should survive a switch, and how compact and wider windows change the navigation surface.

## What to inspect

Read destination count, stable placement, selected-state treatment and the current Expressive guidance together. The inspected page describes three to five peer destinations. It marks the older baseline as no longer recommended and lists web implementations as unavailable; confirm the target implementation before recommending a package.

## What to borrow and adapt

Borrow persistent orientation across views. For a reading app, distinguish Library, Discover and Saved as destinations and preserve useful per-destination position where appropriate. The viewed news example uses labeled icons and a pill-like selected indicator. Adapt the shape, motion and typography to the chosen brand and platform instead of treating the screenshot as a complete style specification.

## Mismatches and limits

A workflow stepper, transient command menu and within-page tabs solve different problems. Compare APG tabs when panels share a page rather than serving as primary app destinations. The example was visually inspected in native Chrome; no destination switching, back-stack behavior or accessibility interaction was tested. Android/Flutter availability does not establish web support, and May 2025 guidance is a source snapshot requiring refresh.

## Related resource roles

- [skill-android-adaptive](skill-android-adaptive.md): An implementation resource with its own SDK and experimental-API boundaries; platform resemblance is not compatibility evidence.

# Primer: action menu boundaries

## When to use

Use when contextual commands need a compact entry point. Ask whether users are executing actions, choosing a value, searching a long set, or filling out a form; those jobs may require different controls.

## What to inspect

Read the boundaries around nested inputs, filterable options and dialog alternatives. Inspect hierarchy, trailing visuals, icon conventions and disabled-item explanations. Primer’s guidance keeps disabled items focusable and provides explanation inline rather than relying on a nested tooltip; adopt this with the selected implementation’s complete keyboard model.

## What to borrow and adapt

Borrow an explicit menu-content contract. For a repository action list, group commands by purpose, use labels that predict results, and reserve trailing space consistently for its chosen meaning. If an item cannot run, explain why at the point of encounter. Move a multi-field setup into a suitable form surface. Compare APG combobox when the true task is supplying an input value.

## Mismatches and limits

Checkmarks, icons and focus treatment must remain coherent with the host system; mixing conventions can make selection and command state ambiguous. Primer-specific icon consistency is a house rule, not proof that every menu needs icons. This card records source guidance only: the menu, submenus, focus navigation and disabled explanations were not exercised. Touch and assistive-technology behavior require composed-product testing.

# Radix: dialog composition and Escape return

## When to use

Use when evaluating a custom-styled React modal or checking whether a proposed wrapper preserves the primitive’s basic interaction. Ask about dismissal, unsaved input, asynchronous completion and where focus should continue.

## What to inspect

Read Root, Trigger, Portal, Overlay, Content, Title, Description and Close together with the focus and dismissal hooks. Inspect controlled state when completion depends on an asynchronous result. The public demo was opened and dismissed: Name received focus, and Escape closed the dialog with focus back on Edit profile.

## What to borrow and adapt

Borrow the explicit composition contract and verify it after applying local styling. For an account editor, connect the title and description, label fields, state how cancellation treats edits, and close only at the chosen transaction outcome. Test keyboard navigation, error reporting, zoom and background interaction in the composed application. An API example is a starting hypothesis for that test.

## Mismatches and limits

The demo’s Save button was not activated; no values were changed and no persistence or network outcome was tested. The receipt covers one open/Escape cycle, not a focus-trap audit or screen-reader conformance. The viewed centered panel and dim overlay are example styling rather than mandatory Radix visual design. A long or complex workflow may deserve a page instead.

## Related resource roles

- [standard-focus-motion](standard-focus-motion.md): A narrowly exercised dialog receipt and broader focus/motion requirements answer different verification questions.
- [tool-axe-core](tool-axe-core.md): Use automated checks only for relevant implemented states, with manual/native evidence where required.

# USWDS: language access by translation coverage

## When to use

Use when people must find content in a language they can use. Ask exactly which pages and tasks are translated, whether a language choice should switch the current page or reveal a collection, and who maintains translation parity.

## What to inspect

Read the complete-coverage and selected-content branches together. The multi-language pattern points to an equivalent page; the partial-coverage pattern exposes a distinct route to available translated material. Both address placement, native language names, right-to-left layout, and avoiding misleading country flags or automatic redirection.

## What to borrow and adapt

Borrow a truthful coverage model. A library site with fully translated account flows can offer equivalent-page switching, while additional translated guides can live behind an explicitly labeled content route. Specify what happens when the current item lacks a translation. Include document-language metadata and real usable destinations; the visible selector alone does not create language access.

## Mismatches and limits

This is a source-described transition, not a tested translation or selector. Exact wording and placement reflect the system and need local comprehension checks. Region, currency and communication preference are different choices and may require separate controls. A preference stored for future messages should not silently imply that all current content is translated. No demo link, language switch or right-to-left rendering was executed here.

## Related resource roles

- [principle-multilingual-layout](principle-multilingual-layout.md): Selection controls and localized layout/script behavior need separate evidence.
- [visual-toss-language-composition](visual-toss-language-composition.md): A narrow observed public language switch provides a comparison, not full accessibility or localization acceptance.

# Separate visual appeal from the task being measured

## When to use

Use when a reference is called universally clean, when a team infers user nationality from aesthetic preferences, or when a visually quiet screenshot is offered as proof that a product will be easier to use.

## What to inspect

Compare the actual tasks: brief appeal ratings versus rapid target finding. Examine sampling, language instructions, different-site stimuli and the distinction between main search and recall analyses. Group-level correlations are different from predictions about an individual.

## What to borrow and adapt

Name the desired outcome before evaluating visual variants. Use visual inspection for hierarchy and character, task observation for retrieval/recovery, and intended-reader judgment for relevance. Remove unnecessary competition for attention while preserving information needed for comparison.

A dense operations table and an exploratory cultural publication can need different compositions even for the same person. The useful question is what attention and work each presentation supports.

## Mismatches and limits

The studies do not prove a universal airy layout, one ideal density, or a style for every person from a particular country. Different real websites vary in more than complexity. A short screenshot exposure does not test learning, error recovery, keyboard operation or prolonged reading. The card is evidence for choosing the right evaluation, not a source of visually inspected product examples.

# Evaluate choice burden in context

## When to use

Use when a team proposes removing options, adding recommendation filters, simplifying a plan selector, or restructuring a reference shortlist because “more choice is bad.”

## What to inspect

Read both meta-analyses' inclusion criteria, outcome definitions and moderators. Preserve the later correction. The earlier near-zero pooled effect and later context-sensitive findings should prompt examination of conditions, not a vote for whichever headline supports the preferred design.

## What to borrow and adapt

Identify the user's knowledge, decision goal, attribute comparability, task difficulty and cost of a wrong selection. Reduce unnecessary effort through explanation, defaults, meaningful grouping or a supported recommendation when appropriate. Retain relevant alternatives and an escape route.

For a workshop catalog, dates and prerequisites may make choices comparable. Hiding half the workshops to meet an arbitrary maximum could remove the only suitable option without reducing uncertainty.

## Mismatches and limits

Historical consumer-choice studies do not determine a universal number of navigation items, cards or model suggestions. Satisfaction, selection rate and task success are distinct outcomes. Do not equate a broad catalog with an overwhelming presentation, or assume a small shortlist is useful when its differences remain unexplained.

# Use alternatives to make critique concrete

## When to use

Use when a person reacts vaguely to one polished direction or cannot describe what they want before seeing possibilities. It is especially useful before expensive commitment to a global visual concept.

## What to inspect

Compare the studies' tasks and controls, not only their titles. Tohidi's alternatives changed ratings and criticism without significantly increasing substantial redesign suggestions. Dow's parallel condition involved nonprofessional ad designers with matched time, prototype count and feedback.

## What to borrow and adapt

Create contrasts that embody a real unresolved decision, with similar content and fidelity. Ask what to keep, change, combine or avoid, then translate those signals into a coherent revision. Alternatives can reveal criticism that politeness or a single polished specimen suppresses.

For a reading club, compare a quiet editorial introduction with a host-led invitation using the same event facts. Let the person identify the relevant relationship instead of requiring them to invent a complete aesthetic.

## Mismatches and limits

Neither study requires three options for every task, a vote on each component or a fixed approval sequence. Lower ratings are not automatically more truthful. Showing options does not itself produce new design ideas, and repeated variations on one template may conceal the real choice. Preserve “neither,” a mixed direction and explicit delegation.

# Elicit the problem from context, not a questionnaire

## When to use

Use when a project owner knows the situation but cannot yet express a design brief, when stakeholders disagree, or when a familiar interface conceals undocumented workarounds.

## What to inspect

Read the roadmap's elicitation techniques and evolution sections together. In the interview guidance, examine prompts about concrete experiences and adaptive follow-ups. The resources concern different roles: end-user research and an owner's creative direction are not interchangeable evidence.

## What to borrow and adapt

Start from supplied material and an actual occasion of use. Ask what happened, what the person tried to accomplish, and which consequence matters. Use a small sketch to expose an unresolved interpretation when words remain too abstract. Maintain a revisable brief instead of completing a rigid intake form.

For a neighborhood event tool, a story about attending alone may reveal a need for host identity and arrival guidance. That is more actionable than asking whether the page should be “modern.”

## Mismatches and limits

These are methodological resources, not proof that interviews alone uncover every need. People may not articulate tacit behavior accurately; observation and artifacts can contradict stated preferences. Do not copy research-session length or consent procedures into every chat, invent user needs from the owner's taste, or delegate all professional design judgment back to the person.

# Request access at the relevant task boundary

## When to use

Use when designing camera, location, notification or other protected-resource requests, especially if onboarding currently asks for every permission before the task is understood.

## What to inspect

Read platform-specific request/denial paths and whether the permission is actually necessary. In the field study, distinguish instrumented access events from sampled retrospective user judgments; a large event log is not an equally large participant sample.

## What to borrow and adapt

Connect a request to the action requiring it, explain the consequence, permit cancellation and preserve unrelated functions. Design denial/revocation as real states. Prefer a supported lower-access alternative when it satisfies the person's task.

For a photo attachment, the permission boundary belongs with selecting or capturing an image, not with a compulsory launch funnel. A refusal should leave the surrounding draft recoverable.

## Mismatches and limits

Android permission families, OS versions and special permissions differ; do not infer current behavior from the 2015 platform. Retrospective preferences are not observed response to a modern prompt. Contextual explanation must not become repeated persuasion until acceptance. This resource does not determine every jurisdiction's consent rules or justify access beyond the requested feature.

# Design name fields for actual naming practices

## When to use

Use when designing registration, event attendance, shipping, account display or another flow that collects or displays people's names across locales.

## What to inspect

Read the scenarios as well as the examples. Distinguish a single-language form used globally from a localized form, and inspect why the application needs each component. The source explicitly warns that naming practices vary within cultures.

## What to borrow and adapt

Collect only the structure the actual task needs. Preserve characters and meaningful ordering, avoid inferring address forms from a presumed Western first/last split, and let people correct how their name is displayed.

For a local club signup, a display name may be enough. A regulated record may have different requirements. Separate those use cases instead of imposing the most elaborate structure on everyone.

## Mismatches and limits

There is no perfect universal field arrangement in this introductory guidance. Do not turn its examples into a closed list of allowed cultures, infer a person's preferred address from nationality, or equate accepting Unicode with complete localization. Security, identity verification and legal record requirements need their own owning sources. This is design/data-model guidance, not evidence that a particular product is culturally inclusive.

# HEART: connect user goals to signals and metrics

## When to use

Use when deciding what would demonstrate that a redesign helped, or when the team is optimizing clicks, sessions or retention without a clear user outcome.

## What to inspect

Read the Goals–Signals–Metrics process and the examples alongside the HEART categories. Inspect how behavioral traces and attitudinal evidence complement each other. The resource's company-scale setting does not make every category mandatory.

## What to borrow and adapt

State the intended user outcome, identify plausible observable signals and alternative explanations, then choose measures that can distinguish them. Keep important dimensions separate.

For a first-event signup, more return visits might mean useful engagement or confusion about where to attend. Completion, correction, arrival confidence and support questions may reveal different aspects of the experience. A concise evaluation can be enough if it addresses the actual decision.

## Mismatches and limits

HEART is a framework with practitioner cases, not a certification or an automatically correct analytics dashboard. It does not prove causal impact from a before/after chart or require instrumenting every available event. Avoid optimizing a proxy whose increase can result from the problem itself. Protect the distinction between reported company experience and measurements collected for the current product.

# Maintain shared direction through feedback and repair

## When to use

Use in an iterative design conversation, particularly when the person gives a partial answer, a short critique, or a correction that affects only part of the direction.

## What to inspect

Read the grounding criterion and collaborative-effort argument together. Inspect how purpose and communication medium change what counts as sufficient understanding. The chapter concerns human coordination rather than prescribing a prompt format.

## What to borrow and adapt

Maintain the distinction between explicit choices, observed constraints and the agent's proposals. Restate only consequential interpretations when doing so makes correction easy. Carry the answered part forward and narrow the unresolved choice instead of restarting the whole brief.

If a person says “keep the warm tone, but the repeated cards feel corporate,” preserve the tone and investigate composition/content treatment. A concrete local revision can expose the interpretation better than another abstract questionnaire.

## Mismatches and limits

Sufficient understanding for one decision is not a permanent complete specification. Silence or elapsed time does not settle a required choice. Minimizing combined effort does not mean minimizing question marks regardless of consequences. The theory does not prove that summarizing every turn helps an agent; use a lightweight working record only when it preserves meaningful direction.

# Design understandable, correctable AI behavior

## When to use

Use for an interface that predicts, recommends, generates or acts with uncertainty, especially when a person needs to correct a result or understand changing behavior.

## What to inspect

Read the guideline groups across first encounter, normal use, mistakes and longer-term adaptation. Inspect the validation method and domain gaps before adopting the paper's broad phrasing as evidence that every guideline applies identically.

## What to borrow and adapt

Make capabilities and likely limits intelligible at the point they matter. Provide efficient dismissal, correction and control. Explain a consequential change without requiring a person to reverse-engineer it, and preserve their ability to recover when automation guesses poorly.

For a suggested meeting plan, distinguish a proposal from a committed booking and make edits local and inspectable. If the system learns from a correction, explain the scope of that adaptation rather than silently changing unrelated work.

## Mismatches and limits

The paper predates contemporary generative-agent workflows. Its practitioner assessment does not prove a numerical productivity or trust benefit for this application. More explanation is not always better, and an explanation does not make a bad action correct. A checklist cannot replace a task/failure model, domain requirements, meaningful user control or actual evaluation.

# Preserve informed choice when optimizing a flow

## When to use

Use when improving conversion, presenting a recommended plan, designing subscription cancellation, or offering creative alternatives whose framing could steer the person toward an unchosen outcome.

## What to inspect

Read the characteristics and examples with the crawl's measurement boundaries. Distinguish an interface's observable choice architecture from a claim about its designer's intent or a measured psychological effect.

## What to borrow and adapt

Make material terms, consequences, alternatives and exit paths legible. Inspect whether a default, wording contrast, visual hierarchy or recovery obstacle changes the choice the person reasonably believes they are making.

For a reference shortlist, do not present one complete attractive concept beside deliberately weak decoys. For cancellation, preserve understandable paths rather than treating successful retention as the only product outcome.

## Mismatches and limits

The historical crawl does not establish present-day prevalence, effect size or legal classification for a particular interface. Text-oriented detection undercovers visual and account-dependent patterns. A strong recommendation is not automatically deceptive when its reason and alternatives are clear. Use the taxonomy to ask precise questions and inspect the full decision, not to assign intent from one screenshot.

# Choose modalities with local users and task evidence

## When to use

Use for a first-time or low-literacy audience, a multilingual field workflow, or a proposed replacement of text with voice or pictograms.

## What to inspect

Read the ethnographic context, task, assistance protocol and participant differences. In the banking comparison, distinguish completion from speed among successful users. Note Wizard-of-Oz speech and experimenter prompts rather than interpreting all completion as unaided success.

## What to borrow and adapt

Investigate the person's language, device familiarity, surroundings, available help and cost of an error. Compare the full task with relevant users. Local graphics, audio, consistent help and human assistance are candidate mechanisms, not an automatic feature bundle.

For a community service, test whether a pictured action means the same thing to participants and whether audio can be heard privately or outdoors. A spoken path can be familiar yet fail if an unfamiliar conversational structure requires the person to infer what to say.

## Mismatches and limits

Historical feature-phone studies do not choose the best modality for today's smartphones or every culture. Text-free does not mean cognition-free; icons are learned and assistance changes outcomes. Do not attach contemporary product claims or a universal voice-first rule to these task-specific findings. The card supplies a research approach, not medical, financial or service-policy advice.
